items.prompt: Which definition matches confirmation bias?

options.label: Favouring information that supports what you already believe
Overestimating how often vivid, memorable events really happen
Believing that past random events change the odds of future ones
Relying too heavily on the first number you encounter when estimating

rubric: Confirmation bias is seeking and favouring information that fits existing beliefs.
The distractors describe availability, anchoring and the gambler's fallacy.

items.prompt: Which definition matches anchoring?

options.label: Leaning too much on the first piece of information
Seeing an outcome as predictable after it has happened
Favouring evidence that supports your existing opinion
Judging likelihood by how easily examples come to mind

rubric: Anchoring is over-reliance on an initial piece of information, such as a first number.
The distractors describe confirmation bias, availability and hindsight bias.

items.prompt: What is the availability heuristic?

options.label: Judging a claim as true by how closely it matches what you already believe
Judging how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind
Judging a past event as having been obvious all along
Judging a price by comparing it with the first price you saw

rubric: Availability means judging frequency or probability by how easily instances come to mind.
The distractors describe confirmation bias, anchoring and hindsight bias.

items.prompt: What term names a systematic, predictable error in human judgment?

options.label: Object permanence
Working memory
Cognitive bias
Classical conditioning

rubric: A cognitive bias is a systematic pattern of error in judgment.
The other terms are real psychology concepts but not about judgment errors.

items.prompt: What is hindsight bias?

options.label: Overrating risks that are easy to picture or recall
Favouring the first option or number you were offered
Feeling an outcome was predictable all along
Seeking only facts that agree with your existing view

rubric: Hindsight bias is seeing outcomes as more predictable once they are known.
Distractors describe anchoring, confirmation bias and availability.

items.prompt: Which of the following are cognitive biases or judgment heuristics? Select all that apply.

options.label: Object permanence
Availability heuristic
Classical conditioning
Anchoring
Confirmation bias

rubric: Confirmation bias, anchoring and availability are standard judgment biases.
Object permanence and classical conditioning are other psychology topics.

items.prompt: A shopper sees a jacket with a crossed-out price of $200 and a sale price of $120. She feels it is a bargain and buys it, without checking what similar jackets usually cost. Which bias is named by the effect of the $200 figure on her judgment?

options.label: Availability heuristic
Confirmation bias
Anchoring
Hindsight bias

rubric: The first price shown acts as an anchor for judging value.
Confirmation and availability involve beliefs and memorable examples, not a reference number.

items.prompt: After a widely reported plane crash, many people say flying feels much more dangerous than driving, though statistics show the opposite. Which idea best explains this?

options.label: Confirmation: they only seek out and read statistics that favour driving
Anchoring: the first statistic they ever heard fixed their later estimate
Availability: vivid, recent cases come to mind easily and seem common
Hindsight: they now believe the crash was obviously foreseeable beforehand

rubric: Vivid news coverage makes examples easy to recall, inflating perceived risk.
Anchoring and hindsight do not fit; nothing suggests a first number or a predictability judgment.

items.prompt: A manager decides early that a new hire is weak. For weeks she remembers every mistake the hire makes and overlooks the successes. Which bias is this?

options.label: Confirmation bias
Availability bias from a vivid news story
Hindsight bias after a project fails
Anchoring on the first salary figure

rubric: She notices and remembers evidence that fits her existing belief.
Other options do not match: no number, no known outcome, no news-driven examples.

items.prompt: Why do cognitive biases occur so consistently across people?

options.label: They appear only when people are very emotional, tired or upset and cannot think clearly
They show a lack of intelligence, so careful and educated thinkers rarely show them
They are deliberate choices people make to defend their pride and protect their image
They come from mental shortcuts that are usually efficient but sometimes err

rubric: Biases are by-products of fast shortcuts that usually work well but err in predictable ways.
The distractors wrongly blame intelligence, emotion or intent.

items.prompt: Which habit is most likely to reduce the effect of anchoring when estimating a house's value?

options.label: Forming your own estimate from comparable sales before seeing the price
Going with your first gut figure as quickly as you can, before doubts creep in
Using the listing price as the baseline and then adjusting slightly up or down
Asking only friends who already like the house for their estimates of its value

rubric: Making an independent estimate first stops the asking price from acting as an anchor.
Starting from the listing price or a quick gut figure keeps the anchor in play.

items.prompt: After an election, a voter says, "I knew all along that candidate would win," although before the vote she was unsure. How should this be classified?

options.label: Hindsight bias
Confirmation bias
Anchoring
Availability heuristic

rubric: Recasting an unsure prediction as certain after the outcome is hindsight bias.
The other biases involve examples, reference numbers or belief-seeking, not rewriting past certainty.

items.prompt: Which strategies can help reduce confirmation bias in your own reasoning? Select all that apply.

options.label: Ask a colleague to argue the opposite position
Write down your prediction and criteria before seeing results
Actively look for evidence that could prove you wrong
Trust your first impression and stop searching
Read only sources that already agree with you

rubric: Seeking disconfirming evidence, opposing views and pre-set criteria counter the pull toward agreeable evidence.
Reading only agreeing sources or stopping early strengthens the bias.

items.prompt: A seller lists a used car at $50,000. A buyer who researched earlier thought it was worth about $35,000, but after seeing the listing she offers $45,000 and feels she negotiated well. What best explains her offer?

options.label: She later felt the sale price was obvious all along
She recalled vivid stories of cars selling for high prices
She searched only for evidence that the car was a bargain
The asking price anchored her sense of what was reasonable

rubric: The high asking price pulled her offer upward from her own earlier estimate, which is anchoring.
The other options need vivid examples, a known outcome or selective searching, none of which appear.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes confirmation bias?

options.label: Letting the first number you hear pull your later estimates toward it, even when it is unrelated
Favouring information that fits your belief and overlooking the rest
Overestimating how common an event is because examples come to mind easily
Feeling after an outcome that you had predicted it all along

rubric: Confirmation bias is the tendency to favour evidence that supports a prior belief.
The distractors describe availability, anchoring and hindsight bias.

items.prompt: A shop marks a jacket "Was $200, now $120", and shoppers say it is a great deal even though similar jackets elsewhere cost $115. Which bias is the shop using?

options.label: Hindsight, because shoppers feel they knew the price would drop
Availability, because shoppers recall other sales easily
Confirmation, because shoppers look for proof it is cheap
Anchoring, because the $200 figure shapes how $120 is judged

rubric: The high original price acts as an anchor that makes $120 seem low.
Confirmation and availability involve evidence-seeking and memory, not a reference number.

items.prompt: After heavy news coverage of a shark attack, many people say swimming in the sea is very dangerous. Why does the availability heuristic explain this?

options.label: People search only for facts that match their fear of the sea
People think the attack was predictable once it had happened
People compare the risk against the first statistic they heard
People judge risk by how easily vivid examples come to mind

rubric: Availability means judging frequency by how readily examples come to mind, and vivid news makes them easy to recall.
Other options describe confirmation, anchoring and hindsight.

items.prompt: Two groups guess a city's population. Group A is first asked, "Is it more than 5 million?" Group B is asked, "Is it more than 500,000?" What will most likely happen?

options.label: Both groups give similar guesses since the question does not matter
Group A guesses lower because they doubt the large figure
Group B guesses higher because small numbers feel more reliable
Group A guesses higher because the large figure pulls estimates up

rubric: Anchoring predicts estimates drift toward the number mentioned first.
Believing the starting figure has no effect ignores how anchors work even when arbitrary.

items.prompt: Psychologists call cognitive biases "systematic" errors. What does this mean?

options.label: They affect only people who have not studied psychology
They lean in a predictable direction in similar situations
They happen at random, so they cancel out over many judgments
They occur only when people are tired or deliberately careless

rubric: Systematic means the errors push judgment in a consistent, predictable direction.
Random-error and carelessness explanations miss that biases occur even in careful people.

items.prompt: Which of these are examples of confirmation bias? Select all that apply.

options.label: Guessing a car's price close to the first figure the seller quoted
Remembering the times a horoscope fit and forgetting the misses
Reading only the reviews that praise a phone you just bought
Fearing flying after seeing a vivid report of a plane crash

rubric: Both selected cases involve favouring evidence that fits an existing belief.
The price guess is anchoring and the flying fear is availability.

items.prompt: On his first day, a coworker tells Mia that the new hire seems lazy. Over the next weeks Mia notices every time he arrives late but does not register the evenings he stays late to finish work. Which explanation best fits her judgment?

options.label: Hindsight bias: after seeing his lateness, she feels she always knew he would be a poor worker
Confirmation bias: she notices evidence that fits the "lazy" label and skips the rest
Availability: late arrivals are vivid and easy to recall, so she overestimates how often he is late
Anchoring: the first number she heard, his lateness in minutes, sets her estimate of his effort

rubric: Mia selectively notices evidence matching the label she was given, which is confirmation bias.
Availability and hindsight do not describe selective attention to supporting evidence.

items.prompt: Before a salary negotiation, Sam wants to avoid being anchored by the employer's first offer. Which step applies that goal?

options.label: Accept the first offer if it feels roughly reasonable
Research typical pay for the role and set a target range first
Wait for the offer and then adjust a little up from it
Ask friends for the one salary they remember hearing about

rubric: Setting your own evidence-based range beforehand gives an alternative reference to the employer's anchor.
Adjusting from the offer is the anchoring pattern itself, and one remembered salary is not systematic.

items.prompt: Lena believes her new study method works. Which action best reduces confirmation bias when she tests it?

options.label: Note each exam where she did well after using the method, to build a record of its results
Read articles that explain why the method should work, written by researchers in the field
Compare her scores with and without the method, including weak results
Ask only classmates who already use the method for their views on how well it works

rubric: A fair comparison includes evidence that could contradict her belief.
The other options gather only supporting evidence.

items.prompt: After several burglary stories on local news, Tom thinks his quiet town is becoming dangerous, though police figures show crime falling. Which response applies the right fix for the bias involved?

options.label: Check actual crime statistics instead of the stories he recalls
Treat the first story he heard as an anchor and adjust his estimate down by half
Search for more news stories to check whether they match his view
Remind himself that the rise in crime was obvious all along in hindsight

rubric: Availability is involved, and replacing memorable examples with actual base-rate data is the standard fix.
Gathering more stories feeds the bias, and hindsight does not apply.

items.prompt: A friend's startup fails, and everyone says, "It was obvious it would fail." Which habit would best reduce this hindsight bias in your own future judgments?

options.label: Avoid following any startup news until the results are known
Rely on the first prediction anyone makes about a startup
Look only for reasons that support the outcome after it happens
Write down your predictions and reasons before the outcome is known

rubric: Recording predictions beforehand prevents memory from being rewritten after the outcome.
Other options either avoid information or increase selective reasoning.

items.prompt: A nurse thinks full moons make the emergency room busier. To test this fairly without confirmation bias, which records should she review?

options.label: Every night, full moon or not, busy or quiet
Only full-moon nights, busy or quiet ones
The nights she remembers most vividly
Only the busiest nights, to count full moons

rubric: A fair test counts all four combinations, including cases that would disconfirm the belief.
The other options use selected or memorable cases only.

items.prompt: A team must estimate a project's cost and wants to reduce anchoring from the client's opening figure. Which steps apply? Select all that apply.

options.label: Have members write independent estimates before any number is shared
Share the client's figure first so everyone works from the same base
Start from the client's figure and adjust until it looks right
Build the estimate from past similar projects' actual costs

rubric: Independent estimates and past-cost reference data avoid dependence on the client's number.
Starting from or sharing the client's figure keeps the anchor in place.

items.prompt: A hiring manager once had a bad hire from a coding bootcamp. Now, reading applications, he skips bootcamp graduates because "they tend not to work out." He has hired only a handful of them. Which step best applies a fix for the bias at work?

options.label: Ask his team which bootcamp graduates they remember doing poorly, to confirm the pattern
Rely on his gut feeling since it comes from his years of hiring experience
Compare performance of all past hires by background, not just the memorable one
Ask colleagues whether they remember any other bad hires from bootcamps they met

rubric: The vivid single case drives an availability error, and checking actual records across all hires corrects it.
Gut feeling and asking for more remembered bad hires reinforce the bias.

items.prompt: A buyer sees a house listed at $500,000 and notices that her own offers keep clustering near that figure. Which step best applies a strategy to reduce anchoring before she negotiates?

options.label: Ask the seller why that price was chosen and use the answer as her main guide
Study the listing price closely until it feels like a fair starting point for talks
Open with an offer well above the listing price to signal to the seller that she is serious
Build her own value estimate from recent comparable sales, setting the listing aside

rubric: Forming an independent estimate from relevant data before seeing the anchor limits its pull.
Distractors keep the listing price as the reference point, so the anchor still shapes the judgement.

items.prompt: After heavy news coverage of a plane crash, Sam plans to drive 600 miles instead of flying. Which action best applies a fix for availability bias?

options.label: Wait a few weeks until the coverage fades, then choose by gut feeling about which is safer
Ask friends which option feels safer and follow the majority view among them
Choose driving, because he can picture the risks of flying much more clearly now
Compare published fatality rates per mile for flying and driving before choosing

rubric: Replacing easily recalled examples with base-rate data counters availability.
Gut feeling or friends' impressions still rely on memorable cases rather than frequencies.

items.prompt: A manager suspects that a new hire is weak. Which step best applies a strategy against confirmation bias in her evaluation?

options.label: Ask team members who share her view to confirm which weaknesses they have noticed
List what evidence would show the hire is strong, then look for it deliberately
Review every task the hire completed and note the mistakes so feedback is specific
Wait until the end of the quarter so that first impressions have time to fade

rubric: Actively seeking disconfirming evidence is the standard remedy for confirmation bias.
Noting only mistakes or asking like-minded colleagues keeps the search one-sided.

items.prompt: A team has spent $50,000 on custom software. Finishing it needs $20,000 more and would deliver $15,000 of value. An off-the-shelf tool costs $10,000 and delivers the same value. Which decision correctly ignores the sunk cost?

options.label: Finish the software, since the $20,000 still needed is less than the $50,000 spent
Finish the software, since the $50,000 already invested would otherwise be wasted
Buy the tool, since it nets $5,000 while finishing the software loses $5,000
Buy the tool and also finish the software so that earlier spending is not lost

rubric: Only future costs and benefits count: tool +$5,000 versus finishing -$5,000.
Other options let the $50,000 already spent drive the decision, which is the sunk cost fallacy.

items.prompt: A project team wants to reduce hindsight bias in its post-project reviews. Which procedure best applies a known remedy?

options.label: Have the most experienced member explain why the outcome was predictable
Hold the review as soon as results arrive, while everyone remembers events clearly
Record forecasts with confidence levels before results, then compare them afterwards
Ask members to recall what they originally predicted once the results are known

rubric: Written pre-outcome forecasts give an unbiased record to compare against.
Recalling predictions after the outcome is exactly where hindsight bias distorts memory.

items.prompt: A hiring panel finds that the first candidate's score sways its ratings of later candidates (anchoring). Which steps apply a sound fix? Select all that apply.

options.label: The first candidate is discussed at length to calibrate the group
Candidates are reviewed in a randomised order for each member
The most senior member shares her rating first to set a standard
Every candidate is scored against the same predefined criteria
Each member scores candidates privately before any discussion

rubric: Independent scoring, varied order and fixed criteria weaken the influence of any single anchor.
Sharing a senior rating first or dwelling on one candidate creates or strengthens an anchor.

items.prompt: A client tells a web team that a redesign 'should take about two weeks.' The team lead must give a realistic estimate and knows the client's figure may anchor the team. Which step best applies a method to limit the anchor's effect?

options.label: Share the client's figure first so the team can explicitly reject it as unrealistic
Choose the estimate closest to two weeks so that the client relationship is preserved
Collect separate estimates based on past similar projects, then compare and combine them
Start from two weeks and adjust upward until the team feels comfortable with the number

rubric: Independent estimates grounded in reference projects reduce reliance on the stated figure.
Adjusting from two weeks or rejecting it explicitly keeps the anchor as the starting point.

items.prompt: After a neighbour's house is burgled, Lena estimates that burglary in her city is far more common than police data show. Which bias best explains this, and why?

options.label: Hindsight: she now believes the burglary was predictable from signs she had noticed
Anchoring: the neighbour's burglary became a reference value she adjusted too little from
Availability: the vivid recent case comes to mind easily, inflating perceived frequency
Confirmation: she searched only for reports that agreed with her earlier view of crime

rubric: Ease of recalling a vivid recent event inflates judged frequency, which is availability.
Other options describe different mechanisms that do not fit a frequency overestimate from one salient case.

items.prompt: A doctor's first impression is flu, with her private probability at 90%. Later blood tests strongly point to a bacterial infection, yet she lowers her flu estimate only to 80%. Which description best identifies the faulty reasoning step?

options.label: She judged flu likely because recent flu cases were easy for her to recall
She later felt the flu diagnosis had been obvious all along, before the tests
She treated her first estimate as a starting point and adjusted too little
She framed the test results as losses, which made her avoid changing course

rubric: Insufficient adjustment away from an initial estimate is the core of anchoring.
Other options name biases about recall, framing or hindsight that the described update does not show.

items.prompt: Staff attended training on confirmation bias, but a year later their error rates are unchanged. Which analysis best explains why?

options.label: Confirmation bias only affects inexperienced staff, so training could not help experienced ones
The staff did not memorise the definitions well enough to recognise the bias as it occurred in their own case decisions
The bias operates automatically, so knowing about it does not change behaviour without process changes
The training was too short, and longer lectures on definitions and examples would have removed the bias entirely

rubric: Biases work largely outside awareness, so structural safeguards such as checklists or devil's advocates are needed.
Other options assume knowledge or experience alone removes the bias, which research does not support.

items.prompt: Two people with opposite views on a policy read the same mixed-results study, and each ends up more convinced of their own position. Which breakdown of the reasoning best explains this?

options.label: Each anchored on the first number reported in the study and ignored the remaining findings
Each scrutinised the disconfirming findings harshly and accepted the supporting ones easily
Each recalled the most dramatic result because it was the easiest one to retrieve
Each judged the study differently because its results were framed as gains for one side

rubric: Uneven scrutiny of supporting and opposing evidence produces polarisation from identical data.
Other options propose mechanisms that would not systematically split two readers by prior view.

items.prompt: In a study, people spin a wheel that lands on 10 or 65, then estimate the percentage of African countries in the UN. Those who saw 65 give higher estimates. Which feature of this result shows anchoring rather than relevant knowledge?

options.label: A random wheel number still pulled estimates toward itself
Both groups guessed above the true value overall
Answers were given as percentages, not as counts
Estimates varied widely within each group, so knowledge differed

rubric: An uninformative number that still shifts judgments is the signature of anchoring.
Other features do not link the estimates to the arbitrary number.

items.prompt: A manager believes a team member is unreliable. Which of her behaviours show confirmation bias at work? Select all that apply.

options.label: Checking the member's logged deadlines against those of peers over six months
Asking only colleagues who have already complained about the member for their opinions
Reading an ambiguous email from the member as proof of carelessness
Asking the member to explain the delays before she reaches a conclusion
Noting each late delivery but treating on-time ones as luck

rubric: Discounting disconfirming cases, sampling one-sided sources and interpreting ambiguity to fit the belief are confirmation bias.
Comparing against peers' data and hearing the member's explanation seek balanced evidence.

items.prompt: Hospital A tells patients that a surgery has a 90% survival rate. Hospital B says the same surgery has a 10% mortality rate. The real outcomes are identical, but more patients at Hospital A choose the surgery. Which analysis best identifies the cause?

options.label: Confirmation: patients at Hospital A searched for reports that supported having surgery
Availability: patients at Hospital A could recall more survivors than those at Hospital B
Framing: equivalent information presented as a gain rather than a loss changes choices
Anchoring: patients adjusted from the 90% figure and underestimated the surgical risk

rubric: Identical facts described as survival versus mortality shift preferences, which is the framing effect.
Other options propose causes that the matched outcomes and wording-only difference do not support.

items.prompt: A client says, "We were hoping for two months." A team then estimates a project at four months, though its last three comparable projects took about nine. Which analysis best explains the estimate?

options.label: Confirmation bias: the team looked only for evidence that supported its own earlier schedule forecast
Hindsight bias: the team now believes the earlier projects were more predictable than they really were
Availability: vivid memories of recent projects made the team underestimate how long this one would take
Anchoring: the client's figure pulled the estimate down, and the team adjusted too little away from it

rubric: The estimate moves toward an externally supplied number and ignores the team's own nine-month history, which is insufficient adjustment from an anchor.
Availability is a tempting distractor, but the recent comparable projects were long, so memory would push the estimate up.

items.prompt: Participants who read a vivid story about a rare disease rate its frequency higher. The rating drops when they must first list twelve examples of similar cases. Which interpretation best fits this pattern?

options.label: Participants became anxious from the vivid story, and the list task distracted them from that anxiety
Judged frequency tracked how easily examples came to mind, and struggling to list twelve made the disease feel rarer
Listing twelve examples gave participants more statistics, so they corrected their estimates using the true base rate
Listing twelve examples exposed the participants' confirmation bias, so they discounted the vivid story as unreliable

rubric: Lower estimates after a hard retrieval task point to ease of retrieval, the availability mechanism, rather than the number of cases recalled.
Distractors substitute general anxiety or base-rate correction, which would not predict a drop caused specifically by retrieval difficulty.

items.prompt: A doctor suspects pneumonia and orders only tests that would be abnormal if pneumonia were present. All come back mildly abnormal, and she confirms the diagnosis. Which step is the specific confirmation-bias error?

options.label: Choosing tests by what the working diagnosis predicts rather than by what could rule it out
Overestimating how common pneumonia is because she treated a severe case last week
Giving more weight to the first symptom reported than to symptoms reported later in the visit
Refusing to change the diagnosis after a test result that clearly contradicted her hypothesis

rubric: Confirmation bias shows up in how evidence is sought: tests that could only support the hypothesis were selected.
Other options describe primacy, availability and belief perseverance, which are different biases; no contradicting result appeared here.

items.prompt: After a product launch fails, a manager says, "The warning signs were obvious." Her written forecasts from before launch were optimistic. Which observation most directly shows hindsight bias?

options.label: She ignored the sales data that disagreed with her written forecasts before the launch
Her memory of her earlier confidence is far more pessimistic than what her documents record
She blames market conditions instead of her own team's decisions for the failure
She now thinks launches like this one will fail more often than her team's past data suggest

rubric: Hindsight bias is a distortion of recalled prior belief, shown by the mismatch between memory and the written record.
Blaming the market is self-serving attribution and overgeneralising from one failure is a different error.

items.prompt: A study profiles ten famous founders who all took huge early risks, and concludes that big risks cause startup success. Which flaw in the reasoning is most fundamental?

options.label: The author sought out founders who confirmed the idea instead of testing the risk hypothesis directly
Vivid stories of famous founders are easy to recall, so the author overestimated how common success is
The sample contains only survivors, so it cannot show whether risk-takers fail more often than others
The author anchored on the first founder profiled and interpreted all the others relative to that case

rubric: Without the failed risk-takers, the sample cannot separate risk from success; this is survivorship bias.
Availability and confirmation are plausible contributors, but the fatal flaw is the missing comparison group.

items.prompt: An analyst reviews studies on whether a policy works. Which behaviours indicate confirmation bias rather than sound reasoning? Select all that apply.

options.label: Lowering confidence in the policy after reading a well-designed study that contradicts it
Scrutinising methods closely in studies with unwelcome results but accepting favourable ones at face value
Using search terms that include the policy's expected benefit, such as "policy improves outcomes"
Checking that a study's sample size is large enough before citing it
Ending the literature search once a few supportive studies are found

rubric: Biased scrutiny, premature stopping and hypothesis-loaded search all tilt evidence gathering or evaluation toward the preferred conclusion.
Updating on strong contrary evidence and applying consistent quality checks are signs of sound reasoning.

items.prompt: A real estate agent shows a buyer a badly overpriced house first and then the house she actually wants to sell, listed at a moderately high price. The buyer calls the second house "a bargain" and offers close to the asking price without checking local sales. What best explains the buyer's judgment?

options.label: The first listing served as a reference point, so the second price was judged against it, not against market data
Availability: the buyer easily recalled vivid recent sales of similar homes and judged this house's price by those memories
Confirmation bias: the buyer looked only for information supporting a decision that was already made before viewing
Hindsight bias: after viewing, the buyer felt the second house's value had been obvious all along and so skipped checking

rubric: The overpriced first listing worked as an anchor and contrast, shaping the price judgment without any market data.
Distractors name real biases, but nothing in the scenario shows memory retrieval, prior commitment or reconstructed beliefs.

items.prompt: You must reply at once to a seller's very high opening price. Your criteria are low cost, usable in the meeting and resistance to anchoring. Which approach best meets them?

options.label: Counter within a fair-value range prepared beforehand from comparables
Stay silent and wait for the seller to concede before judging price
Tell yourself to ignore the number, then judge the price by gut feeling
Offer the midpoint between your budget and the seller's price to keep talks moving

rubric: An independent, pre-set reference range counters the anchor without extra cost during the meeting.
Simply trying to ignore an anchor is weak, and splitting the difference stays tied to the seller's inflated number.

items.prompt: A five-person team must test a hypothesis and decide within a day. Criteria: reduce confirmation bias, little extra time, and still reach a decision. Which procedure is best?

options.label: Before reviewing data, agree on what results would disprove the hypothesis and commit to acting on them
Have each member independently skim the data for a short time, then decide by majority vote on what it shows
Collect as much supporting evidence as possible so the final decision is easy to defend to outside reviewers
Ask everyone to stay objective and consider all evidence equally while reviewing the results, then decide together

rubric: Pre-specifying disconfirming results is cheap and creates a structural check against selective reading.
Exhortations to be objective rarely work, and voting or extra supporting evidence does not address biased evidence search.

items.prompt: A firm claims, "A one-day course listing every cognitive bias will make our staff immune to them." Judged against evidence on debiasing, which evaluation is most defensible?

options.label: Overstated: naming biases helps little in the moment, and process changes like checklists work better
Sound: knowing the names of the biases lets people catch themselves reliably during real decisions
Sound: biases arise from ignorance, so people who know the facts about them stop making the errors
Overstated: bias is purely emotional, so education about thinking can never affect how people decide

rubric: Evidence shows weak transfer from knowledge of biases to behaviour, while structural aids reduce errors more reliably.
Distractors either assume awareness equals immunity or wrongly claim education can have no effect.

items.prompt: A risk officer must rank four decisions by how much they need a safeguard against availability distortion. Criteria: frequency judged from memory, a recent vivid event and no data in hand. Which decision ranks first?

options.label: Setting insurance cover using a ten-year claims database that is reviewed each quarter by the actuarial team
Pricing a product by a formula that the finance team has validated against ten years of historical sales data
Estimating next year's accident risk from memory, right after a dramatic accident in the news
Choosing a security budget from an audit that lists past incidents and their measured costs, drawn up after a recent breach

rubric: Memory-based frequency estimates after a vivid event meet all three criteria and so are most exposed to availability.
The other decisions use records or validated formulas that already limit memory-driven distortion.

items.prompt: A company that completed three similar migrations, each overrunning 40 to 80 percent, plans a fourth. Criteria: accuracy, honesty about uncertainty, and use of past data. Which estimating method is best?

options.label: Average the team members' individual estimates, since combining judgments cancels out their errors
Build a detailed task-by-task estimate and trust it because it reflects this project's specifics
Start from the past overrun range, then adjust explicitly for how this project differs
Add a standard ten percent buffer to the team's estimate, as is common practice

rubric: Starting from the reference class corrects the planning fallacy, and explicit adjustment keeps project specifics in view.
Bottom-up estimates and averaged views share the same optimistic framing, and a small fixed buffer ignores the evidence.

items.prompt: A speaker argues, "Heuristics cause errors, so good decision makers should avoid them entirely." Which are valid criticisms of this claim? Select all that apply.

options.label: Heuristics often give accurate answers in environments that suit them, at a far lower cost than full analysis
Any decision made without heuristics is guaranteed to be free of bias
Better advice is to spot settings where a shortcut fails and use a safeguard there
Avoiding every heuristic is unrealistic, since time and attention limits force people to use shortcuts
Heuristics never lead to systematic error, so the claim's premise is false from the start

rubric: Valid criticisms recognise the efficiency and typical accuracy of heuristics, the impossibility of avoiding them, and the value of targeted safeguards.
Claiming heuristics never err, or that analysis guarantees no bias, overcorrects in the opposite direction.

items.prompt: An emergency department finds clinicians often keep their first diagnosis despite new findings. Management wants a fix that costs little, fits a five-minute handoff and does not ban intuition. Which intervention best fits these criteria?

options.label: Send clinicians to an annual lecture on cognitive biases and diagnostic errors in emergency care
Delay any working diagnosis until the main test results are back, so early impressions cannot anchor
Add a handoff prompt: "What else could this be, and what doesn't fit?"
Have a second specialist review most diagnoses before treatment begins, to catch anchoring errors

rubric: A brief consider-the-alternatives prompt is cheap, fits the time limit and leaves intuition intact while countering anchoring.
Universal second reviews are costly, lectures transfer weakly, and banning early impressions is impractical and loses their value.

items.prompt: A buyer faces a seller's high opening ask on a house. Criteria: low cost, usable in real time, and effective even if the buyer cannot feel the anchor working. Which approach is best?

options.label: Let the seller move first, then adjust step by step from their figure toward what feels like a fair price.
Research comparable sales and set a walk-away price before seeing any ask, then make the first offer yourself.
Remind yourself of anchoring before the meeting, since simply knowing about the bias reliably removes its pull.
Tell yourself the seller's ask is arbitrary and try to ignore it during talks, relying on sheer willpower.

rubric: Preparing an independent reference and setting the first anchor works without depending on awareness.
Distractors rely on willpower, awareness or insufficient adjustment, which are known to be weak against anchoring.

items.prompt: A commentator says: "Heuristics are just errors, so a rational person would never use them." Which critique of this claim is strongest?

options.label: It is flawed, because lab deviations from probability theory show that heuristics fail in most everyday choices, so avoiding them is rational.
It conflates heuristics with biases: in some environments simple rules match or beat complex models, so accuracy depends on fit.
It is flawed, because heuristics are used mainly by novices, and experts replace them with formal calculation as their skill grows over time.
It is flawed, because heuristics are accurate in nearly every setting, and errors arise mainly when people are tired or unmotivated.

rubric: Ecological rationality: heuristic performance depends on the environment, so heuristics are not inherently errors.
Distractors assume lab deviations generalise, that heuristics never fail, or that experts abandon them.

items.prompt: A firm wants to reduce confirmation bias in hiring interviews. Criteria: cheap, scalable, and effective even when interviewers form a quick first impression. Which option is best?

options.label: Let each interviewer form an overall impression first, then probe it with follow-up questions tailored to that candidate.
Give interviewers a one-hour lecture on confirmation bias and trust them to notice and correct it during interviews.
Use a structured interview: same questions for every candidate, each answer scored independently before group discussion.
Give a second interviewer the first one's notes in advance so they can check the first impression and flag any errors.

rubric: Standardised questions and independent scoring limit selective questioning and anchoring on first impressions.
Tailored probing, lectures and shared notes either invite hypothesis confirmation or spread the first impression.

items.prompt: After a failed product launch, a team concludes the warning signs were "obvious all along." Which evaluation of this conclusion is best?

options.label: Reliable if every member independently agrees the signs were obvious, because agreement among members removes the bias and confirms the signals were real.
Reliable: hindsight shows which signals truly mattered, so conclusions drawn after the outcome beat those made beforehand.
Unreliable only for junior staff, since experienced teams are largely immune to the effects of knowing the outcome.
Unreliable: knowing the outcome inflates perceived predictability, so check it against forecasts recorded before the result.

rubric: Hindsight bias makes outcomes seem more foreseeable; pre-outcome records give an unbiased benchmark.
Distractors treat hindsight as insight, assume expertise protects, or treat consensus as a correction.

items.prompt: A risk officer must estimate how often a rare system failure occurs. Which procedure is most exposed to availability bias?

options.label: Use incident rates from a reference class of comparable firms as the starting point for the estimate.
Ask engineers to recall past incidents from memory shortly after a vivid, widely discussed outage.
Use logged incident counts per year over the past decade as the basis for the estimate.
Have engineers review the full logged incident database for the period, then give a frequency estimate.

rubric: Memory-based frequency estimates after a salient event are inflated by ease of recall.
Other options anchor on recorded data or reference classes, which reduce reliance on retrieval ease.

items.prompt: A study claims a one-hour debiasing game "eliminates overconfidence." Participants were tested right after training, on the same game format, with no control group. Which critiques are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: A one-hour session is always too short to affect any bias, so the result must be an error.
Without a control group, improvement may reflect practice or demand effects rather than the training itself.
Immediate same-format testing says nothing about transfer to different tasks or about durability over time.
Overconfidence cannot be measured, so any claim of reducing it is meaningless.

rubric: Missing controls and lack of transfer or delay tests are standard methodological weaknesses.
Overconfidence is measurable through calibration, and short interventions can have effects, so the other critiques overreach.

items.prompt: An emergency physician settles on a first diagnosis from the opening symptoms. Later results are ambiguous, yet she keeps reading them as supporting it. Time is short and tests are costly. Which countermeasure best fits these criteria?

options.label: Defer to the most senior colleague's first impression of the case, because years of clinical experience remove anchoring from diagnostic judgement.
Wait for all lab results before forming any hypothesis, so that no early diagnosis exists to anchor how later findings are interpreted.
Before finalising, state what finding would contradict the working diagnosis and name the best alternative explaining the same symptoms.
Ask the patient to describe the symptoms again and again until a different diagnosis emerges naturally from the account they give.

rubric: Naming disconfirming evidence and an alternative is fast and counters confirmation bias and anchoring.
Withholding hypotheses is impractical, seniority does not remove bias, and re-asking has no principled basis.

items.prompt: A project team keeps underestimating timelines. Design constraints: no new data collection, a quick process, and it must counter the planning fallacy. Which design meets all of them?

options.label: Let the most experienced member set the estimate alone, since expertise removes the planning fallacy from timeline judgement.
Have each member build a detailed bottom-up plan and average the estimates, since averaging cancels individual optimism in the plan.
Have members rate confidence from 1 to 10 and add a fixed time buffer to every task they rate below 5, so doubtful tasks get more slack.
Start from the outcomes of similar past projects, adjust modestly for case-specific features, and record the estimate first.

rubric: The outside view uses existing reference-class data and a recorded estimate to counter inside-view optimism.
Averaging shared optimism does not cancel it; confidence ratings and expertise do not fix the inside view.

items.prompt: A researcher wants to separate confirmation bias from rational belief persistence driven by strong priors. Which study design best does this?

options.label: Ask participants afterwards whether they felt they treated the evidence fairly, since self-reported fairness reveals biased processing.
Compare belief change in people with strong and weak views; smaller change in strong views proves they are biased.
Let participants freely choose evidence sources, then compare their selection and updating with a Bayesian benchmark from their stated priors.
Measure whether participants agree with a hypothesis after reading mixed evidence; any agreement with it shows bias in judgement.

rubric: A normative benchmark from stated priors distinguishes biased search and updating from rational prior-driven persistence.
Other designs confuse strong priors with bias or rely on introspection, which is unreliable.

items.prompt: HR must design an offer process that limits anchoring on candidates' prior salaries. Constraints: consistent across candidates, defensible, and still rewards skill. Which design meets all of them?

options.label: Set pay bands from market data by level before talks, place offers within the band by assessed skill, and exclude prior salary.
Show managers the prior salary beside the band so they can consciously correct away from it when setting the offer.
Let each hiring manager make offers from a personal sense of the candidate's worth, so no fixed reference point exists.
Ask candidates to name a figure first, then discount it by a standard percentage to reach the final offer.

rubric: Pre-set bands give a consistent, independent reference and excluding prior pay removes the anchor.
Intuition varies between managers, candidate-named figures become anchors, and conscious correction is typically insufficient.

items.prompt: A team plans a premortem. The leader presents the plan, then asks the group to discuss aloud, with seniors speaking first, whether anyone fears it might fail. What is the most important missing element?

options.label: Members first write reasons the project failed, assuming it already has, independently and before any discussion.
A longer leader presentation on why the plan is strong, so members have full information before they raise any concerns about it.
A final vote on approving the plan after discussion, so any dissent is formally recorded in the meeting minutes for later review.
Each member announces a numerical success probability publicly, in order of seniority, so the leader can gauge group confidence.

rubric: Independent, prospective-hindsight writing surfaces dissent and avoids conformity and authority effects.
Seniority-ordered statements, advocacy and votes increase conformity and anchoring.

items.prompt: An insurer finds adjusters quote very different premiums for identical cases and wants to measure the problem. Which audit design is best suited to isolating inconsistency (noise), as distinct from average error?

options.label: Have many adjusters price the same case files independently, then compare the spread of quotes within each case.
Train adjusters on anchoring, then survey whether they feel less influenced by irrelevant information when they set their quotes.
Compare the average quoted premium with average claims paid across all cases; a small gap shows adjusters are consistent with one another.
Review rationale memos from the weakest adjusters and replace those whose reasoning appears least convincing to a panel of senior reviewers.

rubric: Noise is the variability among judgments of the same case, measured with a shared-case audit.
An average gap can hide wide scatter, and surveys or memo reviews do not measure inconsistency.

items.prompt: A company wants a review checklist to counter escalation of commitment in struggling projects. Which elements should the checklist include? Select all that apply.

options.label: Ask whether the project would be started today with the same information, ignoring money already spent.
Require the sponsor to defend continuation by listing all the money invested in the project so far.
Agree stop criteria before launch, and have reviewers who did not choose the project assess it against them.
Reward managers for never cancelling a project, to signal that the company values persistence.

rubric: Forward-looking comparison and pre-set criteria with independent reviewers counter sunk-cost reasoning.
Highlighting past spending or rewarding persistence strengthens escalation of commitment.

items.prompt: A news app finds that users who read a story about a rare local crime overestimate how common crime is nearby. The team wants a feature that gives a calibrated view. Constraints: no lectures, honest content, low friction. Which design meets all of them?

options.label: Show a small chart of local crime rates per capita beside the story, as a base-rate reference.
Show a pop-up explaining availability bias and asking users to avoid it before opening the story.
Hide stories about rare crimes so users stop seeing vivid cases that distort perceived crime.
Add emotional language to stories about safe events so they are as memorable as rare crime stories.

rubric: A base-rate display counters availability at the moment of judgement, honestly and with little friction.
Pop-ups lecture, hiding stories is not honest reporting, and emotional embellishment is manipulative.
